evals.prompt: I need to add a feature to our checkout flow that decides whether a cart qualifies for a promotional discount. Marketing wants to configure three things that can each change independently: a minimum cart value, which regions are eligible, and whether it's the customer's first purchase. They also want customer support to be able to see exactly which condition failed when someone asks why they didn't get the discount. Can you help me build this?
evals.expected_output: A solution using verdict's Rule/AndRule/RulesEngine primitives (or a clear justification if not), with per-condition diagnostics available (e.g. via run_all()), not just a single boolean.
expectations: Each of the three conditions (minimum cart value, eligible region, first purchase) is represented as its own independent, named check
A per-condition breakdown is available for the customer-support 'why not' use case, not just a single boolean
Domain logic (cart/discount vocabulary) stays out of low-level rule-evaluation code, or the design explicitly separates the two concerns
A fast pass/fail path and a full-diagnostic path are both addressed as distinct needs, not conflated into one
Config values (minimum, regions) are treated as data that can change without a code edit, not hardcoded literals

evals.prompt: We want to waive shipping fees for an order if ANY of these are true: the order total is above a threshold, the customer has an active premium membership, or they used a valid promo code. Checking the promo code requires calling an external validation service which is slow, so we want to avoid that call whenever possible. How should I structure this?
evals.expected_output: A solution using OrRule (or equivalent short-circuiting logic) with the expensive promo-code check ordered last, and an explanation of why that ordering matters.
expectations: The three checks are combined with OR-like (any-one-passes) semantics
The expensive/slow promo-code check is explicitly ordered last, after the two cheap checks
The solution states or proves that the expensive check is skipped once an earlier check already passes
A test or explicit verification proves the skip actually happens (e.g. a call-counter), not just an assumption that ordering alone guarantees it
The explanation names *why* evaluation order matters (short-circuiting), not just that it happens to work

evals.prompt: We have a growing list of business rules that admins configure through a settings screen (things like category + group membership requirements for feature access). Right now it's a big if/elif function in Python and every time an admin wants a new rule combination, an engineer has to ship a code change. I want to make this configurable from a database table instead. Also, can you write tests to make sure this holds up as the rules grow much more varied? We've been burned by regressions before.
evals.expected_output: A solution building Rule objects from stored configuration data at runtime (not hardcoded), with tests that go beyond a few hand-picked fixtures if the response references verdict's own testing guidance (short-circuit proofs, vacuous-truth cases, or oracle/differential testing).
expectations: Rules are built from external/stored configuration data at runtime, not hardcoded as Python literals
Dispatch on rule/condition type uses a table or polymorphism, not an if/elif ladder keyed on one discriminant
Adding a new rule *combination* (not a new type) is described as a pure data change requiring no code edit
The empty/no-rules-configured case is handled with an explicit, stated decision (not left as an accidental default)

Tests validate correctness across a wide or systematically-varied space of rule combinations, not just a handful of hand-picked fixtures (e.g. property-based testing, an oracle/differential-testing approach, or an equivalently broad technique)
